When to avoid:

1.  Avoid overloading buttons on one page or proximity of two or more buttons to each other, which may create visual overload and difficulty in making decisions.

2. When you wish to direct the user to additional information, you must use the link and avoid using the button.

Recommendations for buttons from the government language characterization guide:

It is recommended to read the dedicated instructions for the buttons in the government language characterization guide -

Guidelines for writing according to situations (harhayeda.gov.il)

Do and Don't
Do
The action of the button must be explained by the text placed on the button. You can add a icon on the button to add relevant information. In addition, you must use up to 1-3 words (2-15 characters) on the button.
Don’t
Don't use two lines of text on a button.
Do
When using multiple buttons, designate the more important action as a primary button and the less important action as a secondary button or text button.
Don’t
Don't use two main buttons side by side.
Do
Use one primary button and let the other buttons be all secondary.
Don’t
Don't use several types of buttons for a section such as primary, secondary and text.

Design
Code
Usage
Accessibility
Accessibility

Contrast Ratio: Ensure the button has sufficient color contrast. The contrast ratio must be at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. You can find the guidelines for color contrast in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum). 

Keyboard Navigation: The button must be fully accessible via keyboard. Ensure that the button can receive focus using the Tab key and can be activated with the Enter or Space keys. This complies with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Focus Indicators: When the button is focused, there must be a visible focus indicator to help users with keyboard navigation. This is required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

Accessible Name: For icon-only buttons, always provide an aria-label that clearly describes the button's function. This adheres to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

Avoid Redundant ARIA Attributes: When using semantic elements like <button>, avoid using redundant ARIA attributes like role="button" or tabindex, which are already inherently included. This follows best practices outlined in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.1: Parsing.

The component is used to select one or more options from a list that opens or closes when clicked.

Design
Code
Usage
Accessibility




Anatomy

Field Label- Text that describes what to expect from the drop-down list of options.

Mandatory Star- Mandatory field marking (Optional).

Tooltip Icon - Icon that opens Tooltip. It is required to create a Tooltip with the additional explanation (Optional).

Question Tooltip- A prompting question that leads to opening a Tooltip. It is required to create a Tooltip with the additional explanation (Optional).

Help Text- We will use critical information that will help complete the operation (available only in Error mode).

Field text- Displays the currently selected option or default prompt.

Field- The element you click on opens the list.

Dropdown Icon- Arrow points up/down, depending on whether the component is open or closed.

List Container- Contains the list of selectable options. Shown in open state.

List Item- One option from the total options displayed in the List Container.

Header- A title that allows you to organize together types of options.

Icon- A symbol that appears at the beginning of the item - (Optional).

Checkbox- In Multi Selection mode, allows the selection of several options.

Select All- In Multi Selection mode, allows marking of all options (Optional).

Remove All- In Multi Selection mode, allows removal of all selected options (Optional).

Clear Icon- The Cancel icon appears in the Filterable Dropdown selection, allowing deletion of the entered Text Field.

Indent - An option that is revealed when its title is opened and will be aligned to the beginning of the heading.

Second Level - The possibility of a title in a more internal hierarchy.

Indent X2 - Like the Indent just one step in the hierarchy.

Icon - An icon that appears at the beginning of the dropdown – optional.

Tags - The selected values ​​are displayed as removable tags.

States
Unfilterable Dropdown

Single Selection Dropdown

Allows selection of one option (when a selection is made the list will close and the Text Field will be updated according to the selection made).

Multi Selection Dropdown

Allows selection of several options. (When the desired options are selected, as soon as we click outside the List Container or click on the Field or the Dropdown Icon, the list will close and the Text Field will be updated according to the selections made).

Filterable Dropdown

Single Selection Dropdown

Allows selecting one option and filtering the list by typing text in the Field (when a selection is made the list will close and the Text Field will be updated according to the selection made).

Multi Selection Dropdown

Allows selection of several options and filtering the list by typing text in the Field (when the desired options are selected, as soon as we click outside the List Container or click on the Field or the Dropdown Icon, the list will close and the Text Field will be updated according to the selections made).

Select All

Clicking Select All will mark all the options in the list.

Remove All

Clicking Remove All will remove all selected options.

Multi Selection With Tags Dropdown

Allows the user to select multiple values ​​from a list using a search box with autocomplete. The selected values ​​are displayed as removable tags, and the list includes check boxes for selecting/deselecting.

Current Page Indicator- Current page

Previous Button- "Back" button for continuous navigation.

States
Behavior

When the carousel contains a large number of items, and users need clear directional controls to navigate the content

When the carousel contains a small number of items, and users can easily understand their location within the carousel.

When the carousel is used on mobile devices or smaller screens where space is limited, and minimalist controls are preferred.

A dialog screen for guiding users through a new product or interface, presenting the core value and main features of the product or service.

Design
Code
Usage
Accessibility
Walkthrough - Modal
Walkthrough - Modal
Walkthrough - Modal
Walkthrough - Modal
Anatomy

Background Overlay - A layer that darkens the rest of the interface. Focuses attention, and prevents interaction with the interface.

Modal Container - A centered dialog box, containing the tutorial content.

Media - Used to display an image or short animation that visually supports a message.

Title - A concise title that presents the purpose of the stage or its main message

Description - Text that explains the element or provides instructions for action.

Action Bottons - Control buttons such as "Next", "Previous", "Skip" or "Close", which allow navigation through the process.

Stage Counter - A step counter that shows the user's position in the guide and helps track progress.

Close Button - Allows the dialogue to be closed at any point in the process.




Types

Moltiple Step's - A tutorial experience that guides the user through a number of actions or functions. It is recommended to limit the number of steps to 3–4 at most.

Single Announcement - A one-time message explaining a new feature or change in the system, without navigation steps.

A fixed navigation component located at the top of the screen, displaying contextual information about the current screen alongside key actions. The component allows users to understand their location in the application structure, navigate back through hierarchical navigation screens, and perform actions relevant to the active screen.

Anatomy

Title – Text indicating the name of the current screen 

Button - Arrow Back – (Optional) Back to previous page button 

Button - Arrow Back + Title – (Optional) Back button and previous page name 

Button – Menu – (Optional) Menu button (less common on iOS)

States






Highlights and differences in the use of the top navigation bar on Android and iOS.
Back Button

iOS

Arrow left, sometimes including the name of the previous screen.

Automatically appears if there is hierarchical navigation.

Android

Arrow left or hamburger menu

The control is in the hands of the designer - can decide whether to show or not

There is a "Back" button as part of the Android system.




Actions - Icon Buttons

iOS

Icons appear only on the left side (in English - on the right side), usually one or two.

Generally, there is no menu.

Android

Support for a menu on the left side that can contain several actions.

There is more flexibility in adding icons.




Scrolling and Sticky Top Navigation Bar

Sticky Top Navigation

When the top navigation bar is set to be sticky and remains attached to the top of the screen during scrolling – a subtle shadow should be added to it. The shadow clarifies to the user that the bar is 'floating' above the scrolling content, and helps to distinguish the boundary between the bar and the content.

Scrolling Top Navigation

When the navigation bar is not sticky, but scrolls together with the content - there is no need for a shadow, as there is no need to create a distinction between the bar and the content beneath it.

Forms

Forms are designed to collect information from the user in a clear and structured way. They can be short or complex with multiple steps and can appear in a variety of formats such as a dedicated page, a section on a page, or a template. Proper design requires planning the structure, selecting appropriate fields, order of presentation, and clear instructions to make it easy for the user to understand and fill out the form easily.

Guidelines
Examples
Instructions for creating a form

Forms are interfaces that are frequently used by citizens. To ensure proper use, rules and good design principles must be respected when designing forms.

*** If possible, it is recommended to use the FG system - the Government Form Generator to build a service form.

Comprehensive design – important to know!
For more details on adapting digital services for users with low digital literacy, visit the attached link.
Designing digital services for a population with low digital literacy

The user must be respected

Forms are designed to collect information and guide the user with as few distractions as possible. To allow the user to scan and complete the form quickly, forms should:

Protect user privacy by only asking for information that is truly needed, so the number of fields required by the user should be reduced to the bare minimum.

Group related tasks under headings to streamline interface scanning.

Maintain a logical and predictable order. For example, first name first, last name next.

Keep a single interaction method as much as possible (e.g., don't require the user to switch between keyboard and mouse multiple times on a single form).

When designing, be aware of password managers and browser capabilities that fill in data for users.

Increase input fields only when they are relevant (and not display them in a Disabled state).

Inform the user when key actions (such as logout) have been clicked and send a confirmation message instead of executing immediately. "You are about to log out. Do you want to save changes before exiting?"

Enable early detection of errors, allow easy correction (completion/autocorrect), and perform automatic saving.




Form structure

Lable - Labels help the user understand what they are required to enter.

Text Inputs - Allows the user to enter free text.

Data Inputs - Input fields that are not free text (e.g. Checkbox, Radio button, Dropdown, File uploader, Date picker, Toggle, etc.).

Help - Provides contextual guidance such as: Tooltip, Placeholder text, Help text, to assist the user in entering the correct information.

Section Header - A title for a section in a form that contains multiple input fields of the same topic.

Buttons - Allows the user to submit or exit the form.



Form building
Regrouping

To help the user understand the form, it is recommended to group fields by topic and give each group a title. In long forms, it is useful to divide the content into clear steps and use a Step Indicator component that shows the user which step they are in and how much is left.

Before moving to the next step, the system will validate the fields that have been filled in.

 Labels

Each input field must include a clear and concise label (1-3 words), to help the user understand what is required of them. Do not use colons after labels, and do not turn the label into help text - keep it short and focused.

Items on a form can be marked as "optional" or "required".

Simple forms

are usually shorter and more user-focused (such as registration forms, contact forms, and payment pages) and most fields will be required.

Complex forms

Depending on the nature of the form, a decision will be made on the number of groups and steps. The goal is to shorten processes to one to three steps (with a maximum of 6 steps) with a clear indication at each step of what is expected to happen and what is required of the user.

Text Inputs

The width of the fields should match the length of the expected content and be adapted to the design grid.

Make sure that the user can enter the information even on small screens.

It is recommended to pre-fill known values ​​in the default state, for example, ID, when possible.

On desktop, up to two fields should be displayed per line, and on mobile – only one field.

Data Inputs

Allow the user to choose from predefined options (such as Dropdown, Radio button, Checkbox). When designing, you should consider the number of options to display, as well as the number of items the user may select. These considerations will determine which component to use.

Help - Offering help

Tooltips

Useful when you need to provide additional optional explanation in a form (rather than an explanation that is required).

Help text

appears below the input field and helps the user provide the correct information. Help text is always available and is therefore a good choice for information that is important to know (in the case of fields next to each other where one has help text and the other does not, the fields should be aligned from the top, not the bottom).

Placeholder text

Provides hints or examples of what to enter. Since the text disappears once the user starts entering data, it should not contain essential information. (Examples should be used instead of real values).

FeedBack

A mechanism in the interface that allows users to receive feedback on actions, content, processes, and interface elements. Through it, we can identify faults, gaps, and systematically improve the system based on user responses.

Guidelines
Examples
Static Feedback

Allows users to provide feedback on informative content without interrupting the flow of use.

1. Feedback message (Trigger)

Placed in a fixed place on the page. The user is not required to search for the element, but will encounter it naturally at the end of reading or scrolling.

Location:

Mostly placed below or next to the content, in order to create a direct connection between the content and the feedback.

Wording:

The wording should be clear, short, and non-marketing.

Use simple icons or visual marking (e.g.: 👍👎).

Example of wording:

Information page on the gov.il website: "Was this page helpful to you? Yes / No

Questions and Answers page: "Was the answer clear? 👍👎

2. Feedback pane open

If the user chose negative feedback, an expanded feedback panel is displayed.

The panel is designed to allow for in-depth and focused feedback, through questions, ratings, and free text.

It is recommended to combine a closed question with multiple choice options and a free text field to focus the feedback and allow for expansion in free language.

For example (closed question on an information page):

I couldn't find the information I was looking for

The information was cumbersome

The information was written in a legal and inaccessible way

3. Thank you message/sending confirmation

Will appear after you submit feedback. For example: "Thank you! Your feedback has been received. We're learning from it to improve the service."

An example of a thank you message, displayed at the end of the process as a thank you for submitting feedback.




Voluntary Feedback

Activated at the user's initiative via a dedicated button or link.

Consists of:

1. Feedback button (Trigger)

Will be positioned in a way that clearly refers to a relevant part of the page.

An example of a feedback button placed in the header and referring to the entire page.

2. Feedback window and confirmation of submission

Opens in the center of the screen above the Overlay layer in the Overlay/default color. Focuses the user on feedback and requires active action to close.




Constant Side-Tab Feedback

Allows users to provide proactive feedback at any time, via a tab located on the side of the screen.

Consists of:

1. Side button/tab button (Tab)

Located on the side of the page and refers to the entire page or service.

Example of a permanent feedback button located on the side of the page

2. Feedback window and confirmation of submission

A feedback panel that opens as a drawer when you click on the tab.

The feedback panel will usually include a closed question, an open question, and submit buttons.

Example of an open feedback panel

Action-Based Feedback

Allows the user to provide immediate feedback after performing an action or completing a process. Appears proactively by the system.

Consists of:

Feedback message and confirmation of sending

The feedback message is displayed below the confirmation message at the end of a process or action (for example: submitting a form, invitation, request).

It is recommended to use closed, short and focused questions.

It is recommended to indicate that the feedback is anonymous to encourage the user's sense of security.

Example of a feedback question that appears at the end of a process

New-Feature Feedback

Designed to provide feedback on a new feature after several uses

Consists of:

Feedback message and confirmation of sending

The feedback message will be displayed close to the time of use of a new feature, usually after 2-3 uses of the feature.

The feedback element should be placed near the feature itself or displayed immediately after the interaction with it.

It is important to make sure that the question refers to a clear, prominent, and identifiable action.

Example of a feedback question about a new feature that appears immediately after using it

FeedBack

A mechanism in the interface that allows users to receive feedback on actions, content, processes, and interface elements. Through it, we can identify faults, gaps, and systematically improve the system based on user responses.

Guidelines
Examples
Static Feedback

Allows users to provide feedback on informative content without interrupting the flow of use.

1. Feedback message (Trigger)

Placed in a fixed place on the page. The user is not required to search for the element, but will encounter it naturally at the end of reading or scrolling.

Location:

Mostly placed below or next to the content, in order to create a direct connection between the content and the feedback.

Wording:

The wording should be clear, short, and non-marketing.

Use simple icons or visual marking (e.g.: 👍👎).

Example of wording:

Information page on the gov.il website: "Was this page helpful to you? Yes / No

Questions and Answers page: "Was the answer clear? 👍👎

2. Feedback pane open

If the user chose negative feedback, an expanded feedback panel is displayed.

The panel is designed to allow for in-depth and focused feedback, through questions, ratings, and free text.

It is recommended to combine a closed question with multiple choice options and a free text field to focus the feedback and allow for expansion in free language.

For example (closed question on an information page):

I couldn't find the information I was looking for

The information was cumbersome

The information was written in a legal and inaccessible way

3. Thank you message/sending confirmation

Will appear after you submit feedback. For example: "Thank you! Your feedback has been received. We're learning from it to improve the service."

An example of a thank you message, displayed at the end of the process as a thank you for submitting feedback.




Voluntary Feedback

Activated at the user's initiative via a dedicated button or link.

Consists of:

1. Feedback button (Trigger)

Will be positioned in a way that clearly refers to a relevant part of the page.

An example of a feedback button placed in the header and referring to the entire page.

2. Feedback window and confirmation of submission

Opens in the center of the screen above the Overlay layer in the Overlay/default color. Focuses the user on feedback and requires active action to close.




Constant Side-Tab Feedback

Allows users to provide proactive feedback at any time, via a tab located on the side of the screen.

Consists of:

1. Side button/tab button (Tab)

Located on the side of the page and refers to the entire page or service.

Example of a permanent feedback button located on the side of the page

2. Feedback window and confirmation of submission

A feedback panel that opens as a drawer when you click on the tab.

The feedback panel will usually include a closed question, an open question, and submit buttons.

Example of an open feedback panel

Action-Based Feedback

Allows the user to provide immediate feedback after performing an action or completing a process. Appears proactively by the system.

Consists of:

Feedback message and confirmation of sending

The feedback message is displayed below the confirmation message at the end of a process or action (for example: submitting a form, invitation, request).

It is recommended to use closed, short and focused questions.

It is recommended to indicate that the feedback is anonymous to encourage the user's sense of security.

Example of a feedback question that appears at the end of a process

New-Feature Feedback

Designed to provide feedback on a new feature after several uses

Consists of:

Feedback message and confirmation of sending

The feedback message will be displayed close to the time of use of a new feature, usually after 2-3 uses of the feature.

The feedback element should be placed near the feature itself or displayed immediately after the interaction with it.

It is important to make sure that the question refers to a clear, prominent, and identifiable action.

Example of a feedback question about a new feature that appears immediately after using it

How do you start working with the governmental design system? All the details here.

UX/UI Design

The government design system has a ready-made component library in the Figma design tool. 

To install the library and quickly and easily pull components into your interfaces, follow these simple steps:

Obtain a Figma License: You can easily order Figma licenses through the Yehalom system. For large organizations, we recommend choosing an Enterprise license, which allows for project management in teams according to the organization's team divisions. Please note: Without a paid license, you cannot use the full capabilities of the system.




Install the Israeli Government Design System Library: First, open the government design system file from the Figma Community. Second, define the file as a Library: In the top menu, click "Publish" to publish the library. And that's it! You have quick access to all components in all organization files, via the Assets tab.

Please Note: Avoid detaching components. If there is a shortage, contact the design system team to complete the shortages comprehensively for all design system users and to maintain consistency.

Contact Racheli at Rachelik@digital.gov.il

When publishing version updates to the government design system, download the design system file from the Figma website again and reinstall it as a library.

Want to stay updated? Join our WhatsApp group: https://did.li/TqPTY




לדיזיין סיסטם הממשלתי יש ספריית רכיבים מוכנה בתוכנת העיצוב Figma. כדי להתקין את הספרייה ולמשוך במהירות ובקלות רכיבים לתוך הממשקים שלכם, יש לבצע מספר שלבים פשוטים:

1.     קבלת רישיון לFigma: ניתן להזמין רישיונות ל-Figma בקלות דרך מערכת יהלו״ם. מבין סוגי הרישיונות, לארגונים גדולים מומלץ לבחור ברישיון Enterprise, המאפשר ניהול של הפרויקטים בצוותים בהתאם לחלוקת הצוותים בארגון. שימו לב: ללא רישיון בתשלום לא ניתן להשתמש במלוא האפשרויות של המערכת.

2.     התקנת Israeli Governament Design System Library: ראשית, יש לפתוח את קובץ הדיזיין סיסטם הממשלתי מתוך Figma Community. שנית, יש להגדיר את הקובץ כ-Library: בתפריט העליון לחצו על "Publish" כדי לפרסם את הספרייה.  וזהו! יש לכם גישה מהירה לכל הרכיבים בכל הקבצים של הארגון, דרך לשונית Assets.

3.     שימו לב: יש להימנע מפירוק קומפוננטות (Detach). אם קיים חוסר, יש לפנות לצוות הדיזיין סיסטם על מנת להשלים את החוסרים בצורה רוחבית לטובת כלל משתמשי הדיזיין סיסטם, ולטובת שמירה על אחידות.

4.     בעת פרסום עדכוני גרסה לדיזיין סיסטם הממשלתי, יש להוריד שוב את קובץ הדיזיין סיסטם מאתר Figma, ולהתקין אותו מחדש כספרייה.

This package contains design tokens that form the basis of IGDS. The tokens define visual aspects such as colors, typography, spacing, and more. They can be used independently in any application to maintain design consistency.

The tokens can be integrated into CSS files or Preprocessor files

The core IGDS package includes custom web components built using Web Components technology and the Lit library.
